title: Testicular Torsion
description: Testicular torsion as a pediatric surgical emergency: presentation in adolescents, absent cremasteric reflex, Doppler ultrasound, the 4-6 hour window to save the testis, preoperative preparation, orchiopexy, and how torsion differs from epididymitis.
keyPoints: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that cuts off blood supply to the testis. It is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY.
Most common in adolescents (peak 12-18 years), with a second smaller peak in newborns. Often occurs during sleep, after activity, or after minor trauma.

Signs: sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain (may radiate to the groin or lower abdomen), scrotal swelling and redness, nausea and vomiting, a high-riding testis with a horizontal lie, and an ABSENT cremasteric reflex.
Doppler (color flow) ultrasound shows decreased or absent blood flow, but if clinical suspicion is high, surgery should not be delayed for imaging.
Surgery within 4-6 hours of symptom onset gives the best chance of saving the testis; viability drops sharply after that. Prepare the teen: NPO, IV access, pain control, consent.
Treatment: surgical detorsion and orchiopexy (fixing the testis to the scrotal wall), usually both sides because the opposite testis is at risk. A nonviable testis is removed (orchiectomy).

Epididymitis has a more gradual onset, often with fever, dysuria, or urethral discharge; pain is relieved by elevating the testis (positive Prehn sign) and the cremasteric reflex is usually present. Torsion pain is NOT relieved by elevation.

questions.stem: Which age group is at highest risk for testicular torsion?

options.text: Toddlers 1-3 years
options.rationale: Torsion is uncommon in toddlers.

options.text: Adolescents 12-18 years
options.rationale: Correct. Torsion peaks during adolescence, when the testes grow rapidly; there is a second smaller peak in newborns.

options.text: School-age children 6-9 years
options.rationale: Torsion can occur at this age but is much less common than in adolescence.

options.text: Young adults over 25 years
options.rationale: Torsion becomes less common after the teen years.

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion most commonly affects adolescents, likely related to rapid testicular growth during puberty and an anatomic predisposition (bell-clapper deformity).

questions.stem: A 14-year-old arrives at the emergency department at 0300 with sudden, severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 1 hour ago. He has vomited twice. The left testis is swollen, high-riding, and lies horizontally, and the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Apply ice and elevate the scrotum, then reassess in 2 hours
options.rationale: Comfort measures do not restore blood flow; waiting reduces the chance of saving the testis.

options.text: Collect a urine specimen for culture and wait for results
options.rationale: A urinalysis may be done but must not delay surgical evaluation.

options.text: Notify the provider at once and prepare for emergency surgery
options.rationale: Correct. Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, and absent cremasteric reflex strongly suggest torsion, which requires surgery as quickly as possible, ideally within 4-6 hours.

options.text: Teach the teen about safer sex practices and STI testing
options.rationale: Teaching about sexually transmitted infections is not the priority during a surgical emergency.

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion is time-critical: testis viability falls sharply after 4-6 hours. The nurse escalates quickly, keeps the teen NPO, starts IV access, gives analgesia as ordered, and prepares for surgery.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a 15-year-old with suspected testicular torsion. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden onset of severe scrotal pain
options.rationale: Correct. Torsion classically presents with sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain.

options.text: Nausea and vomiting
options.rationale: Correct. Nausea and vomiting are common with torsion because of intense pain.

options.text: Absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side
options.rationale: Correct. An absent cremasteric reflex is one of the most reliable signs of torsion.

options.text: Pain relieved when the testis is elevated
options.rationale: Pain relief with elevation (positive Prehn sign) suggests epididymitis; torsion pain is not relieved.

options.text: Gradual onset of pain over several days with burning on urination
options.rationale: Gradual pain with dysuria suggests epididymitis or infection.

options.text: High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
options.rationale: Correct. Twisting of the cord shortens it, pulling the testis up into a horizontal position.

questions.explanation: Torsion: sudden severe pain, swelling, nausea and vomiting, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex. Epididymitis: gradual onset, fever, dysuria, positive Prehn sign, cremasteric reflex present.

questions.stem: The parent of a 13-year-old with testicular torsion asks why the surgeon wants to operate right away. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: The twisted cord cuts off blood flow, and the testis is best saved within 4 to 6 hours.
options.rationale: Correct. The goal is to restore blood flow before tissue dies; salvage rates drop sharply after 6 hours.

options.text: Surgery is needed to drain an infection that has spread into the testis.
options.rationale: Torsion is not an infection; surgery untwists the cord.

options.text: Surgery is done mainly to relieve pain; the testis will heal regardless.
options.rationale: Without prompt surgery, the testis may die and need removal.

options.text: The surgeon needs to remove the testis to prevent it from becoming cancerous later.
options.rationale: Torsion is not related to cancer prevention; the goal is to save the testis.

questions.explanation: Torsion compromises blood flow. Detorsion within 4-6 hours offers the best chance of testicular salvage; delays increase the chance of orchiectomy.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old is diagnosed with testicular torsion and will go to surgery. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.

items.text: Notify the surgeon of the assessment findings
Keep the teen NPO and start IV access
Verify that informed consent has been signed by the parent
Transfer the teen to the operating room

questions.explanation: The surgeon is notified first because time to surgery determines testicular survival. Preoperative preparation (NPO, IV access), comfort, and consent follow quickly so surgery is not delayed.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with sudden scrotal pain is scheduled for a Doppler ultrasound. The teen asks what the test will show. Which response is correct?

options.text: It will show whether there is a kidney stone.
options.rationale: A scrotal Doppler evaluates testicular blood flow, not kidney stones.

options.text: It will measure the size of your bladder.
options.rationale: This test does not evaluate the bladder.

options.text: It will check for a hernia only.
options.rationale: A hernia may be seen, but the main purpose is evaluating blood flow to the testis.

options.text: It shows whether blood is flowing to the testicle.
options.rationale: Correct. Color Doppler ultrasound shows decreased or absent blood flow in torsion.

questions.explanation: Doppler ultrasound helps confirm torsion by showing reduced or absent blood flow, but surgery should not be delayed for imaging when suspicion is high.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing two adolescents with scrotal pain. Which finding is most suggestive of epididymitis rather than testicular torsion?

options.text: Sudden onset of pain that woke him from sleep
options.rationale: Sudden onset is typical of torsion.

options.text: Relief with elevation, plus dysuria and fever
options.rationale: Correct. Pain relief with elevation (positive Prehn sign), dysuria, and fever are typical of epididymitis.

options.text: Absent cremasteric reflex on the affected side
options.rationale: An absent cremasteric reflex suggests torsion.

options.text: High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
options.rationale: This is a classic finding in torsion.

questions.explanation: Epididymitis usually has a gradual onset with fever, dysuria, and pain relieved by elevating the testis. It is treated with antibiotics. When in doubt, torsion is treated as an emergency.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old had a detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy. Which discharge instruction is appropriate?

options.text: Return to contact sports the next day if pain is controlled with ibuprofen
options.rationale: Strenuous activity and contact sports are avoided for several weeks after surgery.

options.text: Remove the dressing and soak in a hot tub on the first day to ease swelling
options.rationale: Soaking is usually avoided until the incisions heal and the surgeon approves.

options.text: No follow-up visit is needed once the incision stops hurting
options.rationale: Follow-up is important to assess healing and testicular viability, even when pain has resolved.

options.text: Wear supportive underwear, use ice for swelling, and limit strenuous activity
options.rationale: Correct. Scrotal support, ice for swelling, and activity restrictions promote healing.

questions.explanation: After orchiopexy, care includes pain control, scrotal support, ice, activity restriction, incision care, and follow-up. The opposite testis is usually fixed too because it is at risk for future torsion.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of adolescent boys about testicular torsion. Which statements indicate the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: If I get sudden, bad pain in my testicle, I should go to the emergency room right away.
options.rationale: Correct. Sudden severe testicular pain is an emergency.

options.text: I should wait to see whether the pain goes away on its own overnight.
options.rationale: Waiting may cause loss of the testis.

options.text: Torsion can happen even when I am sleeping.
options.rationale: Correct. Torsion often occurs during sleep.

options.text: I should tell my parents or coach even if I am embarrassed.
options.rationale: Correct. Embarrassment often delays care; teens should be encouraged to report symptoms promptly.

options.text: Only older men get testicular torsion.
options.rationale: Torsion is most common in adolescents.

questions.explanation: Teens often delay seeking care because of embarrassment. Teaching emphasizes that sudden testicular pain is an emergency and needs immediate evaluation.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old who had torsion for 12 hours before arriving is in surgery, and the testis is found to be nonviable. What will the surgeon most likely do?

options.text: Remove the nonviable testis (orchiectomy) and fix the opposite testis
options.rationale: Correct. A dead testis is removed, and the contralateral testis is fixed (orchiopexy) to prevent future torsion.

options.text: Leave the testis in place and give antibiotics
options.rationale: A necrotic testis is removed; antibiotics are not the treatment.

options.text: Untwist the testis only and do nothing to the other side
options.rationale: The opposite side is usually fixed because of the anatomic risk.

options.text: Postpone surgery until the swelling decreases
options.rationale: Surgery is not delayed in torsion.

questions.explanation: Delayed presentation lowers salvage rates. A nonviable testis is removed, and the other testis is anchored. Teens and families may need emotional support and discussion of a testicular prosthesis later.
